features.label: Donnelly's 'Dolphin's Ridge' (Atlantis)
features.what: Donnelly drew the Atlantis of Plato as a land on the mid-Atlantic ridge next to the Azores, on a map in his book.
features.evidence: The Atlantis of Plato may have been confined to the " Dolphin Ridge " of our map.

position.detail: Book map 'Map of Atlantis, with its islands and connecting ridges, from deep-sea soundings' (printed p. 47, scan page n64, 2174 x 3436 px). Control points: the map's own tick marks, longitude 50, 40, 30, 10 and 0 W (top and bottom, straight fit) and latitude 50 N to 40 S (ten ticks, Mercator fit). Outline traced from the drawn line and simplified to 20 vertices. The map's six Azores dots plot at about 24.2 W, 38.0 N in this grid, about 4 degrees east of the real islands, so the whole drawing is probably shifted by a similar amount. Fit residuals: 0.1 degree in longitude, up to 0.6 degree in latitude.

features.label: 1898 cable-repair dredge (Termier)
features.what: Grappling irons dragged for a broken Brest to Cape Cod cable brought up chips of basalt glass (tachylyte) from rocky sea floor at about 3,100 m.
features.result: Termier read the glass as lava that cooled in air, so land that sank. Schuchert, Day and Pirsson replied that basalt glass forms under water too. The point lies on today's ridge axis, where new lava is erupted.
features.evidence: It was in north latitude 47° 0' and longitude 29° 40' west from Paris, at a point about 500 miles north of the Azores. The mean depth was pretty nearly 1,700 fathoms, or 3,100 meters.

position.detail: Termier (Smithsonian Report 1915 translation, p. 226): 'north latitude 47 degrees 0 minutes and longitude 29 degrees 40 minutes west from Paris'. Converted to Greenwich by subtracting the Paris meridian (2 deg 20 min 14 s east of Greenwich): 27.33 W. Schuchert 1917 prints 29 deg 41 min. If the longitude were Greenwich, the point would be 29.67 W, about 177 km west, and 169 km from the ridge axis. Read as Paris, it lies 0.3 km from the PB2002 axis, which supports that reading.

story.line: 1882: Donnelly draws Atlantis as 'Dolphin's Ridge', a mid-Atlantic land beside the Azores, from nineteenth-century soundings.
1898 to 1912: a cable repair drags up basalt glass 900 km north of the Azores. Termier says it proves recent sunken land.
1917: Schuchert, with Day and Pirsson, replies that basalt glass forms under water too, and the Azores are volcanic, not continental.
1931 and 1944: the ketch Atlantis cruises the Azores, and Pettersson argues continents do not sink and the ridge is building new crust.
1974: Leg 37 drills the ridge at 37 N. The crust is 3 to 16 million years old, basalt under 100 to 450 m of ooze.
1981: Leg 82 drills west of the Azores. The sea floor is 17 to 37 million years old: basalt and gabbro, never a continent.
The real plateau is a swollen volcanic ridge. At 9600 BCE sea level the islands would be only about a quarter bigger.

story.line: 1968: divers off North Bimini report a "pavement" of flat stones in about 5.5 m of water. Edgar Cayce's readings had put Atlantis near Bimini.
Later writers call it a road, a wall or, for Greg Little, a harbour breakwater with a J-shaped end. No open plan of it was found.
Mid-1970s: Eugene Shinn's team cores the stones and cuts the cores to see which way the beach bedding dips.
The bedding dips toward deep water, as on the beach next door, and no tools or artefacts turn up. The stones are beachrock.
Seven radiocarbon dates give 2,750 to 3,510 years. Plato puts the sinking about 11,500 years ago.
Little replies that the stones lie in tiers with prop stones; geologists reply that jointed beachrock can look like this.

story.line: In 2003 Robert Sarmast's book 'Discovery of Atlantis' put the city on the sea bed south-east of Cyprus, a mile down.
In Oct and Nov 2003 a French research ship mapped 20,000 square km of this sea bed and shot seismic lines across it.
In Nov 2004 Sarmast sailed from Limassol for six days of sonar and announced a walled hill with walls 2 to 3 km long.
Within days, geologists said it was an old mud volcano and that they had surveyed the same area the year before.
The survey papers read these hills as salt folds, mud volcanoes and faults; a 2009 paper is reported to find no walls.
Drill cores 200 km west show deep-sea mud, and the Mediterranean last refilled 5.33 million years ago, long before people.

story.line: In the 1920s Bonsor and Schulten dug at Cerro del Trigo for Tartessos. They found Roman remains, and below them only sand and the water table.
In 2004 Kühne, after Wickboldt, read two rectangles in satellite photos of the Hinojos marsh as Plato's temples, and gave their position.
From 2005 the Spanish Hinojos Project drilled cores S7, S9 and S11 to see what lay under the marsh and how old it was.
The cores show a sea-wave sand layer about 4,000 years ago on top of dune sand and old estuary mud. The marsh is much younger than Plato's date.
In 2011 a National Geographic film said radar and resistivity scans found a buried city flooded by a tsunami. The scan positions are not published.
In 2016 core S1 was drilled 0.45 km from Kühne's rectangle: 12 m of marsh mud from 5,000 years ago, with four sandy sea-wave layers.
In 2018 Merlin Burrows named oval 'circles' as Atlantis towers. Critics match them to 96 research ponds dug in 2004 to 2005.

story.line: Ancient writers say a city called Helike, 12 stades from the sea, sank in a winter night in 373 BCE; Pausanias saw drowned ruins.
From 1966 Harold Edgerton's sonar found a target under 42 m of water; three holes drilled in 1973 settled nothing.
In 1988 the Helike Project swept 8 km2 of sea floor with sonar and saw no clear city, so it moved onto land.
On land, 99 boreholes from 1991 found pottery under about 2 km2 of delta between the Selinous and Kerynites rivers.
Digging from 2000 found a Classical building corner 3 m down at Balalas, an Early Bronze Age town 130 m away, and a Roman road.
The finds lie in old lagoon mud now above sea level: the city was buried, then lifted, not found under the sea.
The link to Atlantis stays a proposal: the 373 BCE tsunami layer is only suggestive, and Stiros argues for inland mudflows.

story.line: From 2008, writers and a film said the Richat's rings are Plato's rings of land and water, with the city at the centre.
A 2018 video added numbers: Atlantis 127 stades or about 23.5 km across, mountains to the north, rivers and a flood from the sea.
Geologists had first read the circle as a meteorite crater; fieldwork in the 1960s found no shock rock and the idea was dropped.
The rings are rock ridges, 6, 13 and 20 km across, in a dome over 40 km wide that stands about 420 m above the sea.
Matton and colleagues mapped a 3 km breccia core and dated it, and the carbonate dykes, to about 99 million years ago.
In 2024 six gabbro samples were analysed and two dated by argon: no sharp age, but about 230 to 200 million years, not 99.
Stone tool makers visited long ago: tools lie along the wadis of the outer ring, but no house, wall or canal has been reported.

story.line: In 1939 Marinatos tied the end of Minoan palaces to a Thera eruption. Galanopoulos and Luce later said that eruption inspired Plato's sunken island.
From 1967 Marinatos dug Akrotiri and found a real Bronze Age town under the ash. It proved the eruption but not the Plato link.
Radiocarbon on olive branches from Phira and Therasia dates the eruption to the 17th or 16th century BCE. Plato's date is about 8,000 years earlier.
On Crete, about 155 km away, Palaikastro holds a layer read as a tsunami at least 9 m high, laid down just after the first ash.
Before the eruption the caldera held a shallow lagoon with a central island. Models differ on its shape. It was blown apart; the Kameni islands grew later.
Ships mapped the strait and seismic lines show the sea broke in after the eruption and refilled the caldera in under two days.
In 2023 IODP drilled the caldera floor and the sea around it, to read the ash and flows that Santorini and Kolumbo laid down.

story.line: In 2001 Jacques Collina-Girard proposed that a drowned bank off Cape Spartel was an island at the ice-age low, and the source of Plato's story.
His map shows an island 14 km long and 5 km wide when the sea stood 130 m lower, drowned for good about 11,300 years ago.
In July 2003 the ship Le Suroît mapped the bank with multibeam sonar. We found no open outline of that survey, so none is drawn.
Today's open depth grids put the bank's top about 72 m down, not 56 m, and the 130 m shore much smaller than drawn (our reading of the data).
Gutscher's 2005 paper: a great earthquake and tsunami like Lisbon 1755 is plausible here, and a thick sea-floor mud layer dates to about 12,000 years ago.
Gutscher then wrote that Spartel was the right place but the wrong time, with no Bronze Age society. A 2009 reviewer agreed Atlantis was not found.
